cases.proof: lo starts at 0 and hi starts at n-1; every iteration either lo increases or hi decreases, so lo and hi can move toward each other at most n times combined before lo >= hi ends the loop. Only scalar variables are used.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: Initial window build is O(k); the subsequent loop runs n-k times, each doing O(1) add/subtract work to slide the window by one, giving total O(n) since k <= n. Space is a constant number of scalars.
cases.assumptions: 1 <= k <= a.size(); n = a.size().

cases.proof: right advances exactly once per outer loop iteration for a total of n steps; left only ever moves forward (never resets backward), so across the whole run left's total forward movement is also bounded by n. Each step does O(1) work against the fixed-size 256-entry lookup table.
cases.assumptions: Character values fit in an unsigned char (0-255); n = s.size().

cases.proof: Pointers i and j each advance forward monotonically and independently; the main loop and the two drain loops together perform exactly one O(1) step per element of a and b, visiting each of the n+m input elements exactly once. The output vector stores all n+m merged elements.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(), m = b.size(); both inputs are individually sorted ascending.

cases.proof: fast runs from 1 to n-1 exactly once; slow only ever increases and is bounded above by fast, contributing O(1) amortized work per fast step. Total work is O(n); no extra storage beyond a few scalars is used.
cases.assumptions: a is sorted ascending; n = a.size().

cases.proof: sort costs O(n log n). The outer loop runs O(n) times; for each outer index the inner two-pointer scan does O(n) work in the worst case (converging lo/hi across the remaining suffix). Total is O(n log n) + O(n^2) = O(n^2). Space is dominated by sort's O(n) (or the output triples in adversarial dense-match inputs, which is also bounded by O(n) pairs in typical no-duplicate-heavy inputs, but the sort call itself already establishes O(n) auxiliary space as a baseline).
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); the returned vector of triples is treated as output, not auxiliary, space.

cases.proof: lo starts at 0 and hi starts at n-1; every iteration strictly advances exactly one of them toward the other, so the loop runs at most n times. Only scalar accumulators are used.
cases.assumptions: n = height.size().

cases.proof: The outer loop advances right exactly n times. The inner while loop advances left, but left never resets backward across outer iterations, so left's total advancement over the entire run is also bounded by n. Combined, the amortized total work is O(n).
cases.assumptions: All values in a are non-negative, so windowSum is monotonic non-decreasing as right advances (this guarantees left never needs to move backward); n = a.size().

cases.proof: mid increases on every branch except the swap-with-high branch, and high strictly decreases in that branch instead; the sum (mid's forward progress) + (high's backward progress) is bounded by n, so the loop runs O(n) times total with O(1) work per iteration.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); values are limited to {0, 1, 2}.

cases.proof: The inner pointer j is reset to i+1 at the start of every outer iteration instead of persisting its position, so it does not carry forward progress across outer steps. For an input where the inner while condition holds all the way to n on every outer step (e.g., a strictly decreasing array), each outer iteration costs O(n), giving O(n^2) total in the worst case.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); worst case occurs when a is arranged so a[j] > a[i] holds for the maximal possible range each time.

cases.proof: The step size added to right on each iteration is read directly from a[right] at runtime. If that value is zero, right never advances and the loop does not terminate; if it is negative, right can move backward indefinitely. No invariant in the code guarantees forward progress, so no finite worst-case bound can be derived without knowing the actual data.
cases.assumptions: Bound depends entirely on the runtime contents of a; a well-behaved (all-positive) input would make this O(n / min-jump), but that property is not guaranteed by the code.

cases.proof: lo and hi converge from opposite ends of the string, each iteration moving both by exactly one, so the loop runs at most n/2 times, which is O(n). Only two index scalars are used.
cases.assumptions: n = s.size().

cases.proof: right advances n times total; left never resets backward, so its total advancement across the run is also bounded by n, giving O(n) amortized map operations assuming average O(1) unordered_map insert/erase/lookup. The map holds at most k+1 distinct characters at any time, giving O(k) auxiliary space.
cases.assumptions: Estimated assuming average-case O(1) unordered_map operations (not the pathological worst case with hash collisions); n = s.size().

cases.proof: sort costs O(n log n) and dominates the subsequent single forward pass, which visits each of the n intervals exactly once doing O(1) work per interval. The merged result vector can hold up to n intervals in the worst (no-overlap) case.
cases.assumptions: n = intervals.size().

cases.proof: onStep is an arbitrary caller-supplied callback that may mutate a (e.g., push_back new elements) on every iteration with unknown per-call cost. Because both the loop bound a.size() and the per-iteration cost depend on this opaque callback, no finite worst-case bound can be derived from this function's text alone.
cases.assumptions: Bound depends entirely on the behavior of onStep, which is not visible at this call site.

cases.proof: lo and hi converge monotonically, bounding the number of iterations to O(n); however, shouldAdvance is a caller-supplied function pointer whose internal complexity is unknown at this call site, so the total time is (number of iterations) times (unknown per-call cost), which cannot be reduced to a concrete asymptotic bound without knowing the predicate's implementation.
cases.assumptions: Iteration count itself is O(n), but overall time is Unknown due to the unresolved per-call cost of shouldAdvance.

cases.proof: Each index from 0 to n-1 is pushed onto the deque at most once (in the main loop body) and popped from either end at most once total across the whole run (front-pops for expiry, back-pops for the monotonic property), so total deque operations are O(n) amortized. The deque holds at most k indices at any time.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); 1 <= k <= n.

cases.proof: Prefix sum construction is O(n). In the main loop, each index from 0 to n is pushed onto the deque at most once and popped from the front or back at most once total across the whole run, giving O(n) amortized deque operations. The prefix array uses O(n) space.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); array may contain negative values, which is why a simple two-pointer window (without the deque) would not be correct here.

cases.proof: The worst-case path (no matching pair exists) never triggers the early return, so lo and hi converge over the full range exactly as in the standard converging two-pointer scan, giving O(n) worst-case time. The early return only improves best/average case, not the worst case.
cases.assumptions: n = a.size(); a is sorted ascending. Worst-case bound assumes no pair sums to target.

cases.proof: The loop's only exit condition is right >= n, and right can move backward or stay in place (when a[right] is odd and a[right] resolves the jump back to the same or an already-visited index) with no other variable forcing forward progress. For example, if a[right] is odd and equal to right on some index that is repeatedly revisited, right never reaches n and the loop does not terminate, so no finite worst-case bound can be assigned from the code alone.
cases.assumptions: Bound depends entirely on the runtime values of a; there is no code-level invariant guaranteeing right's forward progress.
